content.intro: This lesson covers Introduction to Software Testing in Rust. It sits in Module 18, Testing, Debugging, and Documentation, and builds toward a practical Rust mental model rather than memorizing a term in isolation.
content.why_it_matters: Introduction to Software Testing in Rust matters when you work with repeatable quality checks and feedback. Understanding the rule helps you predict compiler or runtime behavior, document assumptions, and choose a safer implementation when inputs or system conditions change.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Reliable code uses tests and diagnostics to make assumptions visible. Unit tests isolate behavior, integration tests exercise public boundaries, and documentation tests keep example code checked alongside the API.

content_blocks.title: A reliable way to reason about it
content_blocks.text: For Introduction to Software Testing in Rust, write down the inputs, the guarantee you expect, and the boundary where that guarantee stops. Work through a minimal example first; then deliberately test one edge case. Make tests deterministic and focused. Documentation examples should be executable where possible, and mocks should not obscure the behavior that matters.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not assume Introduction to Software Testing in Rust guarantees more than it actually does. Reduce a failure to a small reproducer, read the full compiler diagnostic or error value, consult the matching official reference, and change one assumption at a time.

content_blocks.title: Toolchain and execution boundary

Most standard-library examples can be tried in a Rust 2024 Cargo project; specialized networking, database, async, procedural-macro, embedded, and WebAssembly scenarios require the toolchain and dependencies described in their lessons.
